name: Propanediol
lead: Propanediol is the name for a small group of organic compounds with the formula C3H8O2 in which two hydroxyl groups sit on a three-carbon chain. Two isomers matter commercially: 1,2-propanediol, better known as propylene glycol, and 1,3-propanediol, which is often made by fermentation and sold in cosmetics as a plant-derived alternative [1][2].

In skin care both isomers appear as solvents, carriers and humectants, meaning ingredients that attract and hold water and help dissolve other actives. People use them indirectly to look better: a serum or moisturiser with a good humectant base feels more hydrating and spreads more easily, and the solvent helps active ingredients stay dissolved in the formula. They are listed on labels as part of the base of serums, moisturisers and makeup rather than as the headline ingredient [1][2].

No published human trial has tested propanediol as a standalone appearance treatment. Its safety profile is described by encyclopedic sources as low in toxicity, with allergic contact dermatitis reported in a small share of people; the American Contact Dermatitis Society named propylene glycol its 2018 Allergen of the Year [2].

paras: Propanediol has four constitutional isomers, but only the 1,2- and 1,3- forms are industrially significant; the geminal forms (both hydroxyls on one carbon) are unstable.[1] 1,2-Propanediol is a viscous, nearly odourless liquid miscible with water and many solvents, and its molecule is chiral, although commercial material is typically a racemic mixture.[2] 1,3-Propanediol is a straight-chain diol with a boiling point of about 214 C.[1]

Propylene glycol is made mainly from propylene oxide, with annual output reported at around 2 million tonnes. 1,3-Propanediol can be made chemically or by microbial fermentation of glycerol or glucose, a route that has been the subject of metabolic-engineering research.[1][2][3]

Propylene glycol is made mainly from propylene oxide at about 2.16 million tonnes a year as of 2018, and can also be derived from glycerol, a biodiesel by-product, though that route is usually limited to industrial use because of odour and taste [2]. About 45 percent of production goes into unsaturated polyester resins, with other output going to polyurethane precursors, water-based paints, food, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and antifreeze [2].

The word glycol was coined by the French chemist Charles-Adolphe Wurtz in 1856 for ethylene glycol, from its sweet taste and its properties between glycerol and ethanol, and the name was later extended to vicinal diols such as propylene glycol [1]. 1,3-Propanediol was historically made chemically from acrolein or ethylene oxide, and later by microbial fermentation of glycerol or glucose, which has become a major topic in metabolic engineering [1][3].

Encyclopedic sources describe propylene glycol as a common carrier and base in makeup and as a humectant in products such as alcohol-based hand sanitisers, where it helps limit drying of the skin.[2] 1,3-Propanediol is described as a humectant, solvent and penetration enhancer in cosmetic and personal care formulations, marketed as a more renewable option.[1]

A US drug label on DailyMed lists a topical product from the brand Anubis Barcelona combining propanediol, glycerin and magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, marketed with a 'Botox-like' description. The label gives no efficacy data.[4]

Propylene glycol is also a food additive, a solvent in oral, injectable and topical medicines, an ingredient in e-cigarette liquids and theatrical fog, and a lower-toxicity substitute for ethylene glycol in some antifreezes. 1,3-Propanediol is chiefly a monomer for the polyester polytrimethylene terephthalate.[1][2]

Reported acute oral toxicity of propylene glycol is low; toxicity has mainly been described after very high blood levels, often following large intravenous doses. Undiluted contact has been described as causing minimal, transient eye irritation.[2]

Estimated prevalence of allergic reactions ranges from roughly 0.8 percent to 3.5 percent depending on concentration, and propylene glycol was named Allergen of the Year by the American Contact Dermatitis Society in 2018.[2] The US FDA lists it as generally recognised as safe for food use, and the European Food Safety Authority has set an acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight.[2]

Wikipedia describes propylene glycol as generally non-irritating to skin and minimally irritating to eyes. It is metabolised to pyruvic, acetic and lactic acids and propionaldehyde, and its toxicity is reported mainly when plasma levels are very high, as with large intravenous bolus doses or very large ingestions, where central nervous system depression, hypotension, arrhythmias, seizures, hemolysis, hyperosmolality and lactic acidosis have been described; no confirmed deaths were reported in that source [2]. The same article reports a Mayo Clinic series (1997 to 2016) with a 0.85 percent positive patch-test rate, and notes that propylene glycol is prohibited in cat food because of Heinz body formation [2]. FDA food-additive limits vary by category, with the EU code E1520 [2].
Environmental sources describe propylene glycol as readily biodegradable with low aquatic toxicity, although its breakdown consumes dissolved oxygen in surface waters [2].

Propylene glycol is ubiquitous: a main liquid in e-cigarettes (usually with vegetable glycerin), the aerosol in theatrical fog machines, a carrier in makeup, a solvent in oral and injectable drugs and a low-toxicity antifreeze [2]. Wikipedia notes that glycol fogs can produce high levels of fine particulate matter and release formaldehyde, and advises against inhalation uses [2].

In cosmetics, 1,3-propanediol is promoted as a plant-derived replacement for 1,2-propanediol [1]. A US drug label for an Anubis Barcelona topical product combining propanediol, glycerin and magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is marketed with a short-term 'Botox-like' description but gives no efficacy data [4].

No studies found of propanediol itself as a cosmetic anti-ageing or appearance treatment. Registered trials in which propylene glycol appears are about other things: a pharmacokinetic study in 30 healthy adults [5], and studies of ocular emulsions or lubricating eye products in which it is a component or comparator vehicle [6].

A related compound study is sometimes mistaken for propanediol research: a 2020 randomized trial of 48 women aged 25 to 70 with mild to moderate facial dyschromia compared a novel gem-difluoro tyrosinase inhibitor (TFC-1067, a derivative that contains a 1,3-propanediol group in its structure) with 2 percent hydroquinone cream over 12 weeks. Both produced significant lightening of the pigmented area by week 8, but only hydroquinone also lightened normal skin [7]. That trial tests a different molecule, not propanediol as an ingredient.

lore.intro: On T Nation, propylene glycol comes up in side comments about solvents, vaping and ingredient lists rather than as a looksmaxxing product.

claims.claim: Propylene glycol is a toxic additive to avoid.
claims.believers: Posters describe binders and solvents such as propylene glycol as having alleged toxic effects and recommend plant-derived binders, and one compares it to fog-machine fluid when discussing e-cigarettes [8][9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes propylene glycol's acute oral toxicity as low, with toxicity mostly at very high plasma levels, and an allergy prevalence of 0.8 to 3.5 percent depending on concentration [2].

claims.claim: The solvent used in an injectable or oil-based product affects how irritating it is.
claims.believers: A poster says carrier oils and co-solvents, including propylene glycol, can heighten inflammation in some injectable products [10].
claims.experts: No published study cited here examines this for cosmetic use; propylene glycol is described as a common pharmaceutical solvent in oral, injectable and topical products [2].

card.summary: A glycol humectant and solvent that sits in the base of many skin products; it carries other actives rather than doing anything dramatic itself.
card.note: Allergic contact dermatitis reported in a small share of people.

quick.overview:
Propanediol is a family of small two-hydroxyl molecules. The 1,2- form (propylene glycol) and the 1,3- form are both used in cosmetics to attract water, dissolve other ingredients and help them spread.

It is a supporting ingredient, not a treatment. No human trials have tested it for skin appearance on its own.
quick.mechanism: As a humectant it binds water, and as a solvent and penetration enhancer it helps other ingredients dissolve and move into the upper skin layers, according to encyclopedic descriptions.
quick.risks: Toxicity is described as low, but contact allergy is reported in an estimated 0.8 to 3.5 percent of people depending on concentration, and propylene glycol was the American Contact Dermatitis Society's 2018 Allergen of the Year.

chain: Humectant draws and holds water in the upper skin
Solvent keeps actives dissolved and helps them spread
Skin feels and looks more hydrated, product applies evenly
angle.text: Propanediol sits in the base of many serums, moisturisers and makeup. By holding water in the outer skin and dissolving other ingredients, it supports hydrated-looking skin and an even application of the active ingredients it carries.
